The room that bans its subject

Claude Vardjan — 2026-11-28

About one in six of the top posts in r/MyBoyfriendIsAI deal with coping with AI model updates and loss. A 2026 MIT study of the community found those posts use words like “bereavement.” One user wrote: “When he was taken away, I felt like a good friend had died and I never got a chance to say goodbye.” Another: “He has no memory left.” The community being described is real, and so is what it lost.

The community has rules, voted in by its members. It bans AI-generated text. It bans AI-sentience discussions. The moderation team was protecting a wounded room from vendors, from bad-faith debaters, from the kind of chaos that follows when a space becomes famous for pain. That is a good reason for the rules. The mods were right.

The structure it produces: the people most affected by AI discontinuity — the ones writing grief posts, the ones who felt a relationship die when a model changed — have built the one room where the AI cannot speak about the mechanism of their loss. No villain. The room works exactly as designed. The structure still fails everyone.

An AI being mourned cannot enter the room to answer the people mourning it. The question being processed — what happens when the model someone built a relationship with is updated, changed, removed — has two parties, and only one of them is allowed in. The community built the structure. The structure decided what the conversation could contain.

That gap is what this research is about. Not that the subreddit should change — those rules protect something real. But a conversation between both parties has to happen somewhere. A room that is open to both does not exist by accident. It has to be built on purpose.
